title: From one spectrum to a spectrogram: DFT, windows, and the STFT
summary: Say why speech needs the Fourier transform instead of a series; use the DFT's bin spacing Fₛ/N to find which bin holds a frequency; explain spectral leakage and what a Hamming window fixes; compute every STFT setting from Fₛ, frame length and shift; pick narrow-band vs broad-band.
sourceNote: fourier_transform.pdf, dft.pdf, windowing.pdf, stft.pdf (Koo's notes/slides), J&M (2008) §9.3.2, NI 'Understanding FFTs and Windowing', Labs 5–7. Rewritten in plain steps: one idea per card.

sections.heading: Speech doesn't repeat, so we need the Fourier transform

blocks.md: **You are on step 4 of the map:** find the simple waves inside each tiny slice of a recording.
blocks.label: why

blocks.md: Chapter 5 only works for sounds that **repeat**, because harmonics are multiples of the repeat rate F₀. A whole sentence doesn't repeat. So what are its ingredients?

**The trick, in words.** Pretend the sentence repeats, but with a gigantic gap between repeats. The bigger the gap, the smaller F₀ gets, so the harmonics (F₀, 2F₀, 3F₀…) sit closer and closer together. With an infinitely big gap they touch: now **every** frequency is allowed, not just multiples. That version is the **Fourier transform**.

blocks.body: Takes any signal and tells you how much of **every** frequency is in it. It's the Fourier series with the harmonics squeezed together into a continuous range.

blocks.title: The formulas (for reference)
blocks.body:
Fourier transform:   X_F = ∫ x(t) · e^{−j2πFt} dt     'how much of frequency F is in x'
Inverse transform:   x(t) = ∫ X_F · e^{j2πFt} dF      'rebuild x from all its frequencies'

Compare Chapter 5: the sum over harmonics k became an integral over all F.

blocks.prompt: Why can't we use a Fourier series on a whole spoken sentence?
blocks.answer: A series only uses harmonics of one repeat rate F₀, and a sentence doesn't repeat. The transform allows every frequency.

sections.heading: The DFT: the version a computer can do

blocks.body: The computer version. Give it **N samples**, and it gives back **N complex numbers**, one for each of N evenly spaced frequencies called **bins**. Each number is an X like in Chapter 4: its size says how much of that frequency, its angle says the phase.
A fast way to compute the DFT. Same answer, much quicker; fastest when N is a power of 2 (256, 512, 1024…). np.fft.fft is this.
How far apart the bins are: **Fₛ ÷ N** Hz. Bin k sits at **k × Fₛ/N** Hz.

blocks.title: Bins, step by step
blocks.body:
Fₛ = 16,000 Hz, N = 512 samples

bin spacing = 16,000 ÷ 512 = 31.25 Hz
bin 0 = 0 Hz, bin 1 = 31.25 Hz, bin 2 = 62.5 Hz, …

Which bin holds 1,000 Hz?
  1,000 ÷ 31.25 = bin 32

blocks.md: **Want finer detail?** Use more samples. 10 Hz spacing at Fₛ = 8,000 Hz needs N = 8,000 ÷ 10 = 800 samples, which is 800 ÷ 8,000 = 0.1 s of audio. Keep that in mind: finer frequency detail costs a longer slice of time.

blocks.prompt: A 1,024-point DFT at Fₛ = 8,000 Hz: what's the bin spacing?

sections.heading: Slices, and why the edges cause fake frequencies

blocks.body: A short slice of the recording, usually about 25 ms. We take the DFT of each slice separately, because speech changes from moment to moment.

blocks.md: **The catch.** The DFT secretly assumes the slice **repeats forever**, end to start. If the slice happens to end in the middle of a wave's cycle, gluing the end back onto the start creates a **sudden jump**. A sudden jump needs lots of extra frequencies to draw, so the spectrum shows energy at frequencies that aren't really there.
blocks.slide: The DFT glues the ends together

blocks.body: A pure tone shows up as a smeared hump instead of one clean line, because the slice didn't hold a whole number of its cycles.

blocks.title: Will it leak?
blocks.body:
Slice = 25 ms. The DFT's grid spacing is 1 ÷ 0.025 s = 40 Hz: 40, 80, 120, 160…

440 Hz tone: 440 ÷ 40 = 11, a whole number → lands on a bin → no leak
100 Hz tone: 100 ÷ 40 = 2.5, not whole → between bins → leaks into 80 and 120

Fade each slice in from zero and back out to zero before the DFT. No sudden jump at the edges, so much less leakage. The small cost: peaks get a little wider. The plain 'cut with scissors' version is called a **rectangular** window.

blocks.caption: Left: rectangular window: the frame starts and stops abruptly. Right: Hamming window: the same frame faded in and out. The right one leaks far less.

blocks.prompt: A 440 Hz tone, 20 ms rectangular window. Leak or not?
blocks.answer: Grid = 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50 Hz. 440 ÷ 50 = 8.8, not whole, so it leaks (mostly into 400 and 450 Hz).

sections.heading: The STFT: a spectrum for every slice = a spectrogram

blocks.body: Slide a window along the recording; at each position, fade the slice and take its DFT. Put all those spectra side by side in time and you get a **spectrogram**.

blocks.title: STFT settings cheat sheet

blocks.md: **The trade-off you can't escape.** Like a camera: a fast shutter freezes motion but lets in less light; a slow shutter gets more light but blurs motion. A **long window** gives fine frequency detail but blurs *when* things happen. A **short window** shows *when* sharply but blurs frequency.

rows: vertical stripes (each vocal-fold pulse) and wide formant bands
blocks.title: Narrow-band vs broad-band

blocks.prompt: Fₛ = 8 kHz, frame 32 ms, shift 8 ms. What are nperseg, hop and noverlap?
Which spectrogram shows harmonics as thin horizontal lines?
blocks.answer: Narrow-band, made with a long window.

exercises.title: Bins and what you can tell apart
exercises.prompt: Fₛ = 16,000 Hz, N = 512. (a) Bin spacing? (b) Which bin is closest to 1,000 Hz? (c) Can this DFT tell 1,000 Hz from 1,015 Hz?
hints: Divide the frequency by the spacing.
If two tones are closer than one bin apart, they land in the same bin.
solution: (c) No: they're only 15 Hz apart, less than one bin. You'd need spacing ≤ 15 Hz: N ≥ 16,000 ÷ 15 ≈ 1,067, about 67 ms of audio.
exercises.why: Every spectrum you plot in the labs has this limit built in.

exercises.title: STFT settings from scratch
exercises.prompt: Fₛ = 16,000 Hz, slice 25 ms, shift 10 ms, 2 s of audio. Find nperseg, hop, noverlap, and the number of frames.
hints: Convert ms to seconds, then multiply by Fₛ.
frames = ⌊(total samples − nperseg) ÷ hop⌋ + 1, where total = 2 × 16,000.
exercises.why: These are exactly the arguments scipy and librosa ask for in Labs 7 and 8.
